claims.text: Hamas won the Palestinian Legislative Council election of 25 January 2006, judged free and fair by international observers; it formed a government on 29 March 2006; donors imposed sanctions, and Egypt and Israel largely closed Gaza's crossings; Israel withheld PA tax revenue and the Quartet ceased aid to a Hamas-led government.

On 25 June 2006 militants crossed from Gaza through a tunnel near Kerem Shalom, attacked an army post, killed two soldiers and captured Gilad Shalit, who was held for more than five years and freed on 18 October 2011 in exchange for 1,027 Palestinian prisoners.

Fatah and Hamas signed the Mecca Agreement on 8 February 2007 and formed a unity government in March; fighting between them on 7–15 June 2007 ended with Hamas in control of Gaza; Abbas dissolved the government on 14 June; the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights reported at least 161 killed; Vanity Fair (David Rose, April 2008) reported documents suggesting a US-backed plan with the PA and Israel to oust Hamas, which Hamas pre-empted; David Wurmser called it 'an attempted coup by Fatah that was pre-empted'; the characterization is contested.

claims.text: On 19 September 2007 Israel's Security Cabinet unanimously declared that Hamas 'has taken control of the Gaza Strip and turned it into hostile territory', citing Qassam fire at Sderot and other communities, and authorized reducing fuel and electricity supplies, restricting goods and restricting movement of people, after legal review and with humanitarian conditions taken into account.

After June 2007 Israel imposed an indefinite blockade; Egypt closed the Rafah crossing in 2007; Israel says the blockade prevents weapons smuggling and rocket fire; dual-use items including construction materials were allowed only for donor projects; virtually all exports were banned; Israeli officials described the export ban as a political decision to separate Gaza from the West Bank; Erez labor permits fell to under 5% of 2000 levels.

Israeli forces seized the Gaza Freedom Flotilla on 31 May 2010, killing nine passengers; in June 2010 Israel eased restrictions to allow nearly all civilian goods while blocking weapons and dual-use items; Rafah partially reopened in June 2010 and opened with limits in May 2011.

The Palmer panel (September 2011) found the naval blockade 'a legitimate security measure' whose implementation complied with international law, found the boarding 'excessive and unreasonable', said no satisfactory explanation had been given for any of the nine deaths, and recommended that Israel continue easing restrictions 'with a view to lifting its closure'.

A January 2008 Israeli document, 'Food Consumption in the Gaza Strip — The Red Lines', estimated that each Gazan needed 2,279 calories a day to avoid malnutrition; it was released in 2012 after a freedom-of-information petition by Gisha; the Defense Ministry said the plan was never implemented.

Since 2006 the permitted fishing zone varied between 3 and 6 nautical miles, occasionally 9 (Oslo envisaged 20); access-restricted areas affected up to 35% of agricultural land and 85% of fishing waters; Israeli fire in them killed 389 and injured 2,829 people between 2007 and 2017; approval of medical exit permits fell from 90% to 62% between 2006 and 2016.

claims.text: Gaza in 2020 (UN Country Team, August 2012): population projected at 2.1 million by 2020; the aquifer 'could become unusable as early as 2016, with the damage irreversible by 2020'; about 90% of its water unsafe without treatment; electricity would need to double; unemployment 29% in 2011 (58% for ages 20–24 in early 2012); the blockade a main reason the economy had not recovered, with losses estimated at $1.9 billion in 2010; economy 'fundamentally unviable under present circumstances'.

Gaza Ten Years Later (UN Country Team, July 2017): unemployment rose from 34.1% (Q1 2006) to 40.6% (Q4 2016), women's from 35.1% to 64.4%; real GDP per capita fell 5.3% (2006–2016) while the West Bank's grew 48.5%; 96.2% of groundwater unfit for human consumption; blackouts of up to 20 hours a day in 2017; food insecurity 47%; 1.2 million people needing humanitarian assistance.

The ICRC said on 14 June 2010 that 'the closure therefore constitutes a collective punishment imposed in clear violation of Israel's obligations under international humanitarian law' and that 'the only sustainable solution is to lift the closure'.
The World Bank estimated Gaza's GDP losses at more than 50% since 2007; poverty was 40% in 2015 with about 80% receiving aid; electricity outages reached 16 hours a day after November 2010.

Israel's Supreme Court in January 2008 upheld the fuel and electricity limitations, holding Israel had no effective control inside Gaza but obligations deriving from the armed conflict, the crossings and the inhabitants' essential humanitarian needs.
